title: Does relation supervision improve compressed scene decisions?
question: Can a 32-scalar scene code retain traversability better when compatibility gradients reach its encoder?
design: 432 procedural scenes in 144 families; 288/72/72 train/validation/test scenes. Three seeds, matched networks and schedules, frozen encoders and fresh probes. Test: 864 pairs, 505 below the clearance requirement.
result: False-safe rate increased from 10.96% to 14.98%; safe recall increased from 77.44% to 84.22%. Paired family-macro difference: +5.81 percentage points [2.54, 9.20].
meaning: The tested relation objective traded safety classification for recall. It did not establish superior task-preserving compression.
limit: False-safe means false accepts / all unsafe candidates. Family-macro and pooled rates have different weighting. Proxy geometry, not execution.
next: Separate the effects of objective, spatial access and representation capacity.

title: Can a stronger global readout recover the missing geometry?
question: Is the problem the compressed representation, regression objective, or how geometry is read?
design: Three scene inputs × three objectives × three seeds: 27 fits. New test draw: 48 families, 144 scenes, 1,728 fixed-bank motion pairs. Accept the highest-ranked 518 candidates.
result: Reconstruction/MSE accepted 22.27% unsafe candidates; relation/Gaussian 19.63%; raw-grid/MSE 28.51%. Local trilinear querying accepted 0/518 unsafe candidates.
meaning: Spatially addressed information was useful where global MLP readers struggled. Raw input size alone did not resolve the bottleneck.
limit: Here risk is unsafe / accepted, unlike the pilot. Raw and compressed readers have different parameter counts. Zero observed errors is not a universal guarantee.
next: Test local access with matched inputs, capacity and relative-position information.

title: Which local information actually helps attention?
question: Do relative spatial coordinates matter under the same local-read budget?
design: Nine fits: uniform pooling, attention without relative XYZ, and attention with XYZ; 6,337 parameters each. Each sphere segment accesses 17 samples × eight grid vertices. Fresh 48-family test draw.
result: At 30% acceptance, unsafe fractions were 7.08%, 10.42%, and 0%, respectively. Deterministic interpolation also had 0/518.
meaning: This local attention design benefited from spatial correspondence and outperformed uniform pooling. It did not beat the analytic reference.
limit: The method still accesses the full 1,400-value grid. It is not a 32-scalar-only representation, nor proof that attention is necessary.
next: Measure additional geometric access and conditioning cost, not just token dimensions.

title: The first conditional flow-matching generator
question: Does local compatibility information improve the distribution of generated motions?
design: Six fits, three seeds per arm, 2,000 updates each. Global scene code versus code plus 12 frozen anchor scores. Fixed 96-control reference pool, 32 generated candidates per scene, Euler16, another fresh 144-scene test draw.
result: Raw valid-candidate yield improved from 50.82% to 54.52%; scenes with a valid candidate from 85.19% to 85.88%. Uniform random sampling yielded 37.20% valid candidates. About 27% of local-FM controls left the declared domain.
meaning: Local conditioning improved this small generator, but domain violations exposed a separate output-parameterization problem.
limit: Outputs are crouch, yaw and lateral shift. Targets are geometry-filtered synthetic controls, not human demonstrations or SONIC tokens. Navigation direction is fixed.
next: Compare bounded coordinates with simple clipping before changing the generative objective.

title: Does better integration make motions more feasible?
question: Are invalid controls a solver problem or an output-distribution problem?
design: Three new tanh-coordinate fits; 33 model/solver/seed evaluations on 48 new families. Compare original FM, terminal clipping and a bounded chart. Retain the same conditioning and candidate count.
result: Valid yield: original Euler16 56.68%; Euler256 52.89%; clipped Euler16 71.69%; tanh FM 71.67%. More steps improved agreement with a Heun numerical reference while increasing domain violations.
meaning: Numerical accuracy and task feasibility are distinct. Bounded training did not establish a yield advantage over clipping: difference −0.03 pp [−1.22, 1.18].
limit: Tanh improved some proxy-cost/diversity diagnostics, not demonstrated navigation. The numerical reference is not an analytic solution. These percentages use a different test draw from the first FM experiment.
next: Keep clipping as a strong baseline; avoid interpreting a legal control range as learned collision safety.

title: Can the reference corpus support native-body supervision?
question: Are body geometry, coordinate frames, references and SONIC formats trustworthy enough for later learning?
design: Read-only inventory and kinematic audits followed by USD re-extraction: 120 Kimodo references, 25,335 frames, 29 ancestry groups, 45 collision shapes. Check 1,016,604 mesh vertices and offline reference packing.
result: USD body positions agree within 5.49e−7 m; mesh envelopes cover the audited vertices. Initially 169/240 scenes were continuously certified, 71 unresolved. 93/120 source clips violate joint limits. SONIC schema, joint-order and packing checks pass.
meaning: The corpus supports typed geometric relations. An offline reference-format test is not a learned native token or execution result.
limit: This is generated Kimodo data, not verified MTC. Authored mesh envelopes are not a physics-cooked collision audit. Unknown outer-envelope overlaps are not collision labels.
next: Recover rejected obstacle candidates, refine interval bounds and retain separate geometric, kinematic and execution labels.

title: Are near-boundary frames the best learning signal?
question: Does emphasizing extreme moments improve learned compatibility?
design: Relabel all 27,000 motion/obstacle pairs: 11,346 clear, 15,066 primitive witnesses, 588 unknown. Eighteen fits cross three class-matched samplers with two pooling methods. Evaluate 4,500 development pairs, accepting 1,350.
result: With attention, witness accepts: uniform 7.06%, low-clearance 6.32%, boundary 8.89%. Direct geometry at the same 16 timestamps has 1/1,350 witnessed false accepts and five unknown accepts. Interval refinement certifies all 240 original scenes.
meaning: Boundary oversampling worsened this implementation. A five-frame torso overlap explains a separate temporal-read failure; it does not validate the sampler.
limit: This is an inspected development set. Unknowns remain separate. Original joint-limit violations remain even after scene certificates improve.
next: Distinguish event exposure during training from choosing informative timestamps at inference.

title: Body aggregation versus temporal query allocation
question: Is risk lost through pooling over body parts, or through missing short time intervals?
design: Nine new fits plus six frozen baselines; four temporal readers at 16 frames × 45 shapes on the same 4,500 development pairs. Include a same-starting-grid static control.
result: Per-body BCE changes witness accepts from 7.06% to 6.40%, with the paired interval crossing zero; distance regression worsens them to 12.35%. Motion-bound reading detects 2,550/2,596 witnesses versus uniform's 2,479.
meaning: Adaptive temporal reads have clearer support than the tested body-loss changes. Detecting a witness, ranking a candidate and certifying clearance are different tasks.
limit: Motion-bound still misses the known five-frame event at budget16. Only 309/4,500 candidates receive a continuous certificate; a low-risk ranking is not equivalent to certification.
next: Measure coverage, abstention and actual stopping cost across budgets on new ancestry groups.

title: Does adaptive reading transfer to new source groups?
question: Can bounded reading improve certification coverage without hiding unresolved candidates?
design: Freeze 20 additional Kimodo ancestry groups: 20 clips, 3,930 frames, 4,500 pairs. Compare 8/16/32/64 queries and run real early stopping. Keep the old development cohort separate.
result: At64, motion-bound certifies 1,666/4,500 versus static time-gap's 829, a +18.60 pp gain [15.24, 22.02]. It detects all 2,450 known witnesses and leaves 384 unresolved. Mean stopped reads fall from 29.56 to 19.38.
meaning: The certificate/abstention interface transfers to additional groups of the same generated corpus.
limit: At16, endpoint reading detects more 1–5-frame witnesses: 107/124 versus 95/124. Seventeen new clips retain joint-limit violations. The known five-frame case is detected by motion-bound at query24, not retroactively at16.
next: Connect frozen FM outputs to the checker and retain exact continuous geometry as a strong baseline.

title: Does query efficiency improve frozen-FM output?
question: Does a budgeted checker improve end-to-end valid yield per unit compute?
design: Three frozen fits, 48 fresh procedural families, 144 scenes, 32 candidates each: 13,824 candidates. Preserve original 21-knot paths. Compare 72 method/budget/seed cells with independent continuous replay.
result: Motion-bound early stopping: 9,147 valid accepts, 357/432 valid returns, 19.65 point queries per candidate. Exact: 9,962 accepts and 375/432 returns. Assembled cost is about 48.6 ms per valid return for both.
meaning: Fewer queries alone did not establish a pipeline advantage; the exact checker retained more outputs.
limit: The 432 evaluations repeat 144 scenes across models. Sampled-only checking at16 actually selects seven invalid motions. A float32/float64 geometry mismatch was corrected with all arms rerun; decisions were unchanged.
next: Send only unresolved candidates to fresh exact checking, with identical output sets as the acceptance criterion.

title: Can exact fallback retain yield while reducing cost?
question: Can cheap certificates remove enough exact work to pay for themselves?
design: Reuse the same 13,824 candidates; seven arms × three models × three shuffled timing repetitions =63 records. Recompute geometry on every invocation; no truth lookup in operational fallback.
result: Every arm accepts the same 9,962 candidates and makes identical selections on 375/432 valid returns. Uniform16 + fallback checks 6,419 candidates exactly. Checker cost: 38.147 → 20.136 ms per valid return; assembled pipeline: 58.603 → 40.592 ms.
meaning: A simple hybrid is a provisional lower-cost validation option. Motion-bound16 reduces exact work further but its prefilter overhead makes it slower here.
limit: Reused development bank; three descriptive timing repetitions. Common generation-stage timings are reused, not remeasured end-to-end. Raw FM validity remains 72.06%.
next: Freeze the provisional choice for replication and diagnose generation failures before adding new learned mechanisms.
